meta.note: Original CISSP-style practice questions. matching questions carry a prompts[] (left items numbered 1..n) and options[] (right items A..n); correct_answer encodes the pairing. sequence_ordering correct_answer lists option labels in correct order.

questions.question: A core principle for secure software development is that security and privacy should be:

options.label: A
options.text: Left entirely to the end users

options.label: B
options.text: Added only after the software is in production

options.label: C
options.text: Integrated at every phase of the SDLC, not bolted on at the end

options.label: D
options.text: Considered only during the disposal phase

explanation.why_correct: Security and privacy must be built in at every SDLC phase (requirements through disposal); change control is especially critical during O&M.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Bolting on security post-production is costly and leaves gaps.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Security must apply throughout, not only at disposal.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Security is a shared responsibility led by the development organization.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the build-security-in-at-every-phase principle.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Software Development Security > Software Development Lifecycle

questions.question: Order the following SDLC phases from earliest to latest. (Provide the option labels in order.)

explanation.why_correct: The SDLC proceeds from requirements/initiation, to design, development, testing, deployment, operations & maintenance, and finally disposal.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the ordered SDLC phases.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Software Development Security > Key Phases of SDLC

questions.question: During the Operations and Maintenance (O&M) phase, which control is described as especially critical?

explanation.why_correct: Change control is critical during O&M to ensure updates/patches do not introduce security weaknesses or instability.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Marketing analysis is unrelated to O&M security.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Office planning is a facilities task.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Recruitment is an HR function.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps O&M-phase rigor to change control.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Software Development Security > Important Considerations

questions.question: The Waterfall model is characterized by:

options.label: A
options.text: Continuous, overlapping iterations with no defined phases

options.label: B
options.text: Delivering working software every two weeks by default

options.label: C
options.text: A sequential approach where each phase is completed before the next begins (with limited feedback loops)

explanation.why_correct: Waterfall is a sequential model: one phase must finish before the next starts, with only limited feedback (e.g., testing back to a prior step). Its rigidity is a noted drawback.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Continuous overlapping iteration describes Agile, not Waterfall.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Two-week deliveries describe Agile sprints.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Waterfall is documentation-heavy, not documentation-free.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the sequential nature of Waterfall.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Software Development Security > Software Development Methodologies Part 1

questions.question: The Spiral model is BEST known for:

options.label: B
options.text: Emphasizing iterative development with repeated risk analysis in each cycle

explanation.why_correct: The Spiral model combines iterative development with explicit, repeated risk analysis at each loop/cycle, making it well-suited to high-risk projects.

why_others_are_wrong.A: The Spiral model is inherently iterative.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Requirements are still essential in the Spiral model.
why_others_are_wrong.C: It differs from Waterfall by adding iteration and risk focus.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps repeated risk analysis to the Spiral model.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Software Development Security > Increment Build Model

questions.question: The Cleanroom development model focuses primarily on:

options.label: B
options.text: Rapidly prototyping with end users in JAD sessions

options.label: C
options.text: Preventing defects through rigorous design/verification rather than relying on after-the-fact testing

options.label: D
options.text: Skipping design to start coding immediately

explanation.why_correct: Cleanroom emphasizes defect prevention and correctness via formal methods and rigorous review, aiming to avoid introducing defects rather than finding them later.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Rapid prototyping with users describes RAD/JAD.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Cleanroom is design-rigorous, not design-skipping.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Outsourcing is unrelated to the Cleanroom approach.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps defect prevention/correctness to the Cleanroom model.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Software Development Security > Software Development Methodologies Part 2

questions.question: The Joint Application Development (JAD) model is characterized by:

options.label: B
options.text: A purely solo developer working in isolation

options.label: D
options.text: Structured collaborative workshops/sessions involving stakeholders to define requirements

explanation.why_correct: JAD uses facilitated, collaborative sessions ("JAD sessions") with stakeholders to rapidly define and refine requirements together.

why_others_are_wrong.B: JAD is collaborative, not solo.
why_others_are_wrong.A: JAD specifically involves stakeholders/customers.
why_others_are_wrong.C: JAD is a requirements-gathering technique, not its elimination.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps collaborative requirement workshops to JAD.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Software Development Security > Joint Application Development (JAD) Model

questions.question: A team needs to quickly produce a working prototype to validate an idea with users, iterating fast. Which methodology is MOST suited?

explanation.why_correct: RAD emphasizes rapid prototyping and iteration (often with JAD and CASE tools), ideal for quickly building and validating prototypes.

why_others_are_wrong.C: Waterfall's rigidity is poorly suited to rapid prototyping.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Cleanroom prioritizes formal correctness over rapid prototyping.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Skipping methodology invites disorganized, risky development.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps rapid prototyping needs to RAD.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Software Development Security > Rapid Application Development (RAD) Model

questions.question: The Incremental Build model develops software by:

options.label: A
options.text: Delivering the entire system only once at the very end

options.label: D
options.text: Building it in smaller, manageable increments, learning from each to improve the next

explanation.why_correct: The Incremental Build model constructs software in increments, allowing learning from prior increments to improve later ones (it resembles Agile but predates it).

why_others_are_wrong.A: A single end delivery describes Waterfall, not incremental build.
why_others_are_wrong.C: It enables system engineering during analysis/design.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Incremental development specifically adapts based on prior increments.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps incremental, learn-as-you-go development to the Incremental Build model.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Software Development Security > Increment Build Model

questions.question: Which statement reflects a core value of the Agile Manifesto?

options.label: A
options.text: Responding to change over following a rigid plan

options.label: C
options.text: Processes and tools over individuals and interactions

explanation.why_correct: Agile values responding to change over following a plan (and individuals/interactions, working software, and customer collaboration over their counterparts).

why_others_are_wrong.B: Agile values working software over comprehensive documentation.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Agile values customer collaboration over contract negotiation.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Agile values individuals and interactions over processes and tools.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests an Agile core value.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Software Development Security > Agile Development

questions.question: A team is adopting Agile and wants to ensure security keeps pace with rapid iterations. The BEST approach is to:

options.label: A
options.text: Define security controls upfront and integrate them (and configuration management) into the Agile process

options.label: B
options.text: Let each developer decide security individually with no standards

options.label: C
options.text: Defer all security work until a final security phase after release

options.label: D
options.text: Skip security because Agile moves too fast for it

explanation.why_correct: Security should be defined upfront and integrated into each iteration (along with configuration management), rather than deferred—keeping security continuous in Agile.

why_others_are_wrong.C: Deferring security to a final phase contradicts Agile's iterative delivery and leaves risk.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Agile and security are compatible; security must be integrated, not skipped.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Ad-hoc per-developer security yields inconsistent, weak controls.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests integrating security into Agile iterations.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Software Development Security > Security in Agile

questions.question: In Scrum, which role is primarily responsible for facilitating the process and removing impediments for the team?

explanation.why_correct: The Scrum Master facilitates the Scrum process and removes impediments; the Product Owner manages the backlog/priorities, and the development team builds the product.

why_others_are_wrong.D: The Product Owner owns the backlog and priorities, not impediment removal/facilitation.
why_others_are_wrong.A: A DBA is not a defined Scrum role.
why_others_are_wrong.B: A CFO is not a Scrum role.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps facilitation/impediment removal to the Scrum Master.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Software Development Security > Scrum Methodology in Agile

questions.question: The Sprint Retrospective in Scrum is used to:

options.label: B
options.text: Reflect on the completed sprint and identify process improvements for the next one

explanation.why_correct: The retrospective is a continuous-improvement ceremony where the team reflects on what went well/poorly and adjusts for the next sprint.

why_others_are_wrong.C: Demonstrating the product is the sprint review.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Initial requirements precede sprints (in the backlog).
why_others_are_wrong.A: Automated deployment is a CI/CD activity, not the retrospective.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the improvement purpose of the retrospective.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Software Development Security > Sprint Lifecycle and Process

questions.question: A project has stable, well-understood, unchanging requirements and strict documentation needs (e.g., a regulated system). Which methodology is MOST appropriate?

options.label: D
options.text: Pure Agile with no fixed requirements

explanation.why_correct: Waterfall suits projects with stable, well-defined requirements and heavy documentation/regulatory needs, where sequential phases work well.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Agile shines with evolving requirements; here requirements are stable/fixed.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Ad-hoc development lacks the rigor regulated systems require.
why_others_are_wrong.C: RAD's rapid churn fits prototyping, not a stable, documentation-heavy effort.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps stable, documentation-heavy requirements to Waterfall.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Software Development Security > Choosing a Development Methodology (Review)

questions.question: Which TWO are principles of the Agile Manifesto? (Select TWO.)

options.label: A
options.text: Resist any requirement changes after the start

options.label: B
options.text: Measure progress only by lines of documentation

options.label: C
options.text: Welcome changing requirements, even late in development

explanation.why_correct: Agile principles include delivering working software frequently and welcoming changing requirements; working software (not documentation volume) measures progress.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Agile welcomes requirement changes rather than resisting them.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Working software, not documentation volume, measures progress.

questions.exam_reasoning: Identifies Agile Manifesto principles.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Software Development Security > Agile Manifesto - 12 Principles

questions.question: Match each development methodology (1-4) to its defining characteristic (A-D).

options.label: A
options.text: Rapid prototyping, often with JAD and CASE tools

options.label: B
options.text: Sequential phases completed one before the next

options.label: C
options.text: Iterative cycles with repeated risk analysis

explanation.why_correct: Waterfall → sequential phases (B); Spiral → iterative with risk analysis (A); RAD → rapid prototyping with JAD/CASE (D); Cleanroom → defect prevention via verification (C).

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests mapping of methodologies to their characteristics.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Software Development Security > Choosing a Development Methodology (Review)

questions.question: Which TWO are Agile core values (the preferred side of the comparison)? (Select TWO.)

options.label: C
options.text: Individuals and interactions (over processes and tools)

options.label: D
options.text: Following a fixed plan (over responding to change)

explanation.why_correct: Agile values individuals/interactions and working software (also customer collaboration and responding to change) over their counterparts.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Agile values responding to change over following a fixed plan.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Agile values customer collaboration over contract negotiation.

questions.exam_reasoning: Identifies the preferred Agile values.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Software Development Security > Agile Development

questions.question: A noted drawback of the Waterfall model is that:

options.label: A
options.text: It is rigid—changes are difficult and costly once later phases begin

explanation.why_correct: Waterfall's sequential rigidity makes accommodating changes late in the project difficult and expensive, a primary drawback.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Waterfall delivers once at the end, not frequently.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Waterfall has clearly defined sequential phases.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Waterfall is planning-heavy, not planning-free.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the rigidity drawback of Waterfall.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Software Development Security > Software Development Methodologies Part 1

questions.question: Security activities during the SDLC disposal phase should ensure that:

options.label: A
options.text: New features are added before retirement

options.label: B
options.text: The system runs indefinitely without review

options.label: C
options.text: Source code is published publicly by default

options.label: D
options.text: Data is securely sanitized and the system is decommissioned without leaving recoverable sensitive data

explanation.why_correct: The disposal phase securely sanitizes/destroys data and decommissions the system so no sensitive data remains recoverable.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Adding features is a development/maintenance activity, not disposal.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Disposal ends the system's life rather than running it forever.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Publishing source by default is not a disposal security goal.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests secure data handling at the disposal phase.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Software Development Security > Software Development Lifecycle

questions.question: Which of the following is an Agile methodology/variant?

explanation.why_correct: Scrum is a widely used Agile framework; Waterfall, Cleanroom, and JAD are non-Agile (or pre-Agile) approaches.

why_others_are_wrong.C: Waterfall is a sequential, non-Agile model.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Cleanroom emphasizes formal defect prevention, not Agile iteration.
why_others_are_wrong.D: JAD is a collaborative requirements technique, not an Agile framework.

questions.exam_reasoning: Identifies Scrum as an Agile methodology.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Software Development Security > Other Agile Methodologies

questions.question: NIST publications on the SDLC emphasize that across the lifecycle phases, organizations should:

options.label: B
options.text: Integrate security and privacy considerations consistently into each phase

options.label: D
options.text: Treat security as optional after deployment

explanation.why_correct: NIST SDLC guidance stresses integrating security and privacy at every phase, with consistent processes and documented phase outputs.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Security is not optional; it must be continuous.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Documenting phase outputs is part of sound SDLC practice.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Skipping testing increases the risk of vulnerabilities.

questions.exam_reasoning: Reinforces consistent security integration per NIST SDLC guidance.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Software Development Security > NIST Special Publications

questions.question: Midway through development, a key customer requirement changes significantly. How does an Agile team ideally respond, per Agile principles?

options.label: A
options.text: Refuse the change because the plan is fixed

options.label: B
options.text: Ignore the customer and ship the original scope

options.label: C
options.text: Welcome the change and incorporate it in an upcoming iteration, even late in development

explanation.why_correct: Agile welcomes changing requirements—even late—harnessing change for the customer's competitive advantage by incorporating it in an upcoming iteration.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Refusing change contradicts Agile's responding-to-change value.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Canceling overreacts; Agile adapts to change.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Ignoring the customer contradicts customer collaboration.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests Agile's welcoming of late requirement changes.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Software Development Security > Agile Manifesto - 12 Principles

questions.question: DevSecOps differs from DevOps in that DevSecOps:

options.label: B
options.text: Removes security entirely to speed delivery

options.label: D
options.text: Integrates security into the DevOps pipeline ("security as code"), shifting security left

explanation.why_correct: DevSecOps embeds security throughout the DevOps pipeline ("security as code"), automating security testing and shifting security earlier ("shift left").

why_others_are_wrong.B: DevSecOps adds security; it does not remove it.
why_others_are_wrong.A: It applies to software pipelines, not hardware manufacturing.
why_others_are_wrong.C: DevSecOps integrates dev, sec, and ops collaboration—not staff replacement.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the security-integrated nature of DevSecOps.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Software Development Security > DevSecOps Overview

questions.question: In a DevOps environment, developers gradually accumulate pipeline permissions from past projects. Which controls BEST address this?

options.label: A
options.text: Share one privileged account across the team

options.label: B
options.text: Enforce least privilege and separation of duties with role-based access to avoid authorization creep

options.label: C
options.text: Disable all access controls in the pipeline

options.label: D
options.text: Grant everyone administrator access for convenience

explanation.why_correct: Least privilege, separation of duties, and clear role-based access controls prevent authorization (privilege) creep in DevOps pipelines.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Universal admin access violates least privilege and expands risk.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Disabling access controls is dangerous.
why_others_are_wrong.A: A shared privileged account destroys accountability.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps authorization-creep mitigation to least privilege/SoD/RBAC.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Software Development Security > Security and Access Controls in DevOps

questions.question: Continuous Integration (CI) primarily involves:

options.label: A
options.text: Frequently merging code changes into a shared repository with automated build/test

explanation.why_correct: CI frequently integrates code into a shared repo, triggering automated builds and tests to catch issues early.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Annual manual deployment is the opposite of continuous practices.
why_others_are_wrong.D: CI relies on automated testing.
why_others_are_wrong.C: CI depends on version control.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the frequent-merge/automated-test nature of CI.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Software Development Security > CI/CD Pipeline and Security Integration

questions.question: How does Continuous Deployment differ from Continuous Delivery?

options.label: A
options.text: Continuous Deployment automatically releases passing changes to production; Continuous Delivery stops at a deployable artifact awaiting approval

options.label: B
options.text: They are identical in every way

options.label: D
options.text: Continuous Delivery automatically deploys to production with no gate

explanation.why_correct: Continuous Delivery produces a release-ready artifact that requires a manual approval to deploy; Continuous Deployment automatically pushes passing changes all the way to production.

why_others_are_wrong.B: They differ at the final release gate.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Continuous Delivery typically includes an approval gate before production.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Continuous Deployment relies on automated testing to gate releases.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes Continuous Deployment (auto-to-prod) from Continuous Delivery (gated).

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Software Development Security > CI/CD Pipeline and Security Integration

questions.question: Embedding security into a CI/CD pipeline (DevSecOps) is BEST achieved by:

options.label: A
options.text: Letting only one person see the pipeline

options.label: B
options.text: Removing automated tests to speed the pipeline

options.label: C
options.text: Involving security at each pipeline stage with automated security testing

options.label: D
options.text: Running a single manual security review only after release

explanation.why_correct: Security should be involved at every pipeline stage with automated security testing (e.g., SAST/DAST, dependency scanning) so issues are caught continuously.

why_others_are_wrong.D: A single post-release review misses issues introduced earlier.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Removing tests increases the risk of shipping vulnerabilities.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Restricting visibility to one person harms collaboration and review.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests integrating automated security throughout CI/CD.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Software Development Security > Security in CI/CD Pipelines

questions.question: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) improves security and consistency by:

options.label: A
options.text: Defining infrastructure in version-controlled code so it is repeatable and auditable

options.label: B
options.text: Eliminating the need for access controls

options.label: D
options.text: Configuring every server manually by hand

explanation.why_correct: IaC declares infrastructure in code (version-controlled), enabling consistent, repeatable, auditable, and reviewable provisioning—reducing configuration drift and manual error.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Manual configuration is error-prone and inconsistent—the problem IaC solves.
why_others_are_wrong.C: IaC manages changes; it does not prevent them.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Access controls still apply to IaC pipelines and infrastructure.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the repeatable/auditable benefit of IaC.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Software Development Security > DevOps and DevSecOps

questions.question: The Capability Maturity Model Integration (CMMI) defines how many maturity levels?

explanation.why_correct: CMMI defines five maturity levels (typically Initial, Managed, Defined, Quantitatively Managed, and Optimizing), used to assess and improve process maturity.

why_others_are_wrong.A: CMMI has five, not three, levels.
why_others_are_wrong.B: CMMI has five, not seven, levels.
why_others_are_wrong.C: CMMI has five, not ten, levels.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of CMMI's five maturity levels.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Software Development Security > Capability Maturity Model Integration (CMMI)

questions.question: The IDEAL model's five phases stand for:

explanation.why_correct: IDEAL stands for Initiating, Diagnosing, Establishing, Acting, and Learning—a model for guiding process improvement.

why_others_are_wrong.A: These are not the IDEAL phases.
why_others_are_wrong.C: These are not the IDEAL phases.
why_others_are_wrong.D: These are not the IDEAL phases.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of the IDEAL phases.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Software Development Security > Software Maturity Models

questions.question: The OWASP Software Assurance Maturity Model (SAMM) is used to:

options.label: A
options.text: Analyze and improve an organization's software security posture across the SDLC

options.label: B
options.text: Encrypt data at rest on servers

options.label: D
options.text: Provide backup power to build servers

explanation.why_correct: OWASP SAMM helps organizations assess and improve their software security posture and integrate security strategy throughout the SDLC.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Data-at-rest encryption is a separate control.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Backup power is a UPS/generator function.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Packet routing is a network function.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps software-security maturity assessment to OWASP SAMM.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Software Development Security > Software Assurance Maturity Model (SAM)

questions.question: Software maturity models are used to:

options.label: A
options.text: Provide physical security for data centers

options.label: B
options.text: Assess and improve the effectiveness/consistency of an organization's software development processes

options.label: C
options.text: Replace the need for any testing

explanation.why_correct: Maturity models evaluate how effective and consistent development processes are and provide a path to improve them.

why_others_are_wrong.D: They assess processes; they do not encrypt code.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Testing remains necessary regardless of maturity level.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Physical security is unrelated to software maturity models.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the process-improvement purpose of maturity models.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Software Development Security > Software Maturity Models

questions.question: Order the patch management process steps as described in the guide. (Provide the option labels in order.)

explanation.why_correct: Patch management proceeds: Evaluation, Testing, Approval, Rollout, and Verification.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the ordered patch management process.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Software Development Security > Patch Management Process

questions.question: Regression testing during O&M ensures that:

options.label: A
options.text: The software has the most marketing appeal

options.label: B
options.text: New patches or changes have not broken previously working functionality

options.label: C
options.text: The build server has redundant power

explanation.why_correct: Regression testing verifies that applied changes/patches have not adversely affected existing functionality.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Marketing appeal is unrelated to regression testing.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Documentation is still valuable; regression testing does not preclude it.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Build-server power is unrelated to regression testing.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the purpose of regression testing.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Software Development Security > Regression and Regression Testing

questions.question: During O&M, continuous monitoring helps identify:

options.label: D
options.text: Unauthorized patches or backdoors and other emerging security issues

explanation.why_correct: Continuous monitoring during O&M can detect unauthorized changes (e.g., rogue patches or backdoors) and emerging vulnerabilities.

why_others_are_wrong.C: Holiday schedules are unrelated.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Marketing metrics are unrelated to O&M monitoring.
why_others_are_wrong.A: The cafeteria menu is irrelevant.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the security value of continuous monitoring in O&M.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Software Development Security > Continuous Monitoring in O&M

questions.question: A vendor releases an urgent security patch for a production application. Before broad rollout, the team should:

options.label: A
options.text: Deploy it to production immediately with no testing

options.label: B
options.text: Test the patch in a non-production environment and obtain approval via change control

options.label: D
options.text: Apply it only to the developer's laptop and consider it done

explanation.why_correct: Patches should be evaluated, tested in non-production, and approved through change control before rollout and verification—balancing security with stability.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Untested production deployment risks outages from a faulty patch.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Ignoring an urgent security patch leaves a known vulnerability exposed.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Patching one laptop does not protect production systems.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests test-then-approve-then-rollout patch practice.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Software Development Security > Patch Management Process

questions.question: An Integrated Product Team (IPT) brings together which kind of membership to improve outcomes?

options.label: A
options.text: Only the most senior executive, working alone

options.label: B
options.text: Cross-functional stakeholders (e.g., development, security, operations, business) collaborating on the product

options.label: D
options.text: Exclusively external contractors with no internal staff

explanation.why_correct: An IPT is a cross-functional team (development, security, operations, business, etc.) that collaborates throughout the product lifecycle to improve quality and alignment.

why_others_are_wrong.A: A lone executive is not a cross-functional team.
why_others_are_wrong.D: IPTs integrate internal stakeholders, not only external contractors.
why_others_are_wrong.C: IPTs span multiple functions, not marketing alone.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the cross-functional nature of IPTs.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Software Development Security > Integrated Product Teams

questions.question: A code repository (e.g., using Git) primarily provides:

options.label: B
options.text: Version control, change tracking, and collaboration for source code

options.label: D
options.text: Physical access control to the office

explanation.why_correct: Code repositories manage code versions, track changes, and enable team collaboration (e.g., Git with GitHub/GitLab/Bitbucket).

why_others_are_wrong.A: Backup power is a UPS/generator function.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Physical access control is a facility control.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Wireless encryption is WPA2/WPA3.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the version-control/collaboration purpose of code repos.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Software Development Security > Code Repositories

questions.question: A developer is about to commit a file containing API keys and database passwords to a PUBLIC code repository. What is the security concern and best practice?

options.label: A
options.text: Secrets should always be committed for convenience

options.label: B
options.text: Public repos automatically encrypt secrets, so it is safe

options.label: C
options.text: Hardcoding secrets is fine if the repo is popular

options.label: D
options.text: Secrets must not be stored in (especially public) repos; use secret managers and remove/rotate exposed secrets

explanation.why_correct: Storing secrets in repositories—especially public ones—exposes them to anyone; secrets should be kept in secret managers, and any exposed secrets must be removed and rotated.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Public repos do not encrypt content; anyone can read committed secrets.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Repo popularity increases, not decreases, exposure risk.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Committing secrets is a serious security mistake.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the no-secrets-in-repos best practice.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Software Development Security > Security Considerations for Code Repositories

questions.question: In Git, which operation uploads local commits to a remote repository?

explanation.why_correct: git push uploads local commits to the remote repository; git init creates a new repo and git clone copies a remote repo locally.

why_others_are_wrong.A: git init initializes a new local repository.
why_others_are_wrong.D: git clone copies a remote repository to the local machine.
why_others_are_wrong.C: ".gitignore" excludes files; "git ignore" is not the push command.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of git push (upload to remote).

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Software Development Security > Basic Git Operations (Example)

questions.question: "Shifting security left" in DevSecOps means:

options.label: A
options.text: Addressing security earlier in the development lifecycle rather than only at the end

options.label: C
options.text: Moving servers physically to the left side of the room

explanation.why_correct: Shifting left moves security activities earlier (design, coding, build) so issues are found and fixed sooner and more cheaply.

why_others_are_wrong.C: It is a metaphor about timing, not physical placement.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Shifting left is the opposite of deferring security.
why_others_are_wrong.D: It adds earlier security testing, not removes it.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the meaning of shifting security left.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Software Development Security > DevSecOps Overview

questions.question: The Capability Maturity Model (CMM/SW-CMM) helps an organization to:

options.label: A
options.text: Assess the maturity of its software process and chart improvements toward higher levels

options.label: B
options.text: Provide fire suppression in server rooms

explanation.why_correct: CMM evaluates software-process maturity and provides a staged path to improve process capability over time.

why_others_are_wrong.C: Traffic encryption is a separate control.
why_others_are_wrong.D: CMM improves processes; it does not replace developers.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Fire suppression is a physical control.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the maturity-assessment purpose of CMM.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Software Development Security > Software Maturity Models

questions.question: Which TWO are benefits of a well-designed CI/CD pipeline with integrated security? (Select TWO.)

options.label: A
options.text: Elimination of the need for any version control

options.label: B
options.text: Earlier detection of vulnerabilities through automated security testing

options.label: C
options.text: Faster, more consistent and repeatable releases

options.label: D
options.text: Removal of all human oversight from releases

explanation.why_correct: CI/CD with integrated security yields faster, repeatable releases and earlier vulnerability detection via automated testing.

why_others_are_wrong.A: CI/CD depends on version control, not its elimination.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Human oversight/approval gates remain important, especially for production.

questions.exam_reasoning: Identifies CI/CD-with-security benefits.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Software Development Security > Security in CI/CD Pipelines

questions.question: DevOps primarily aims to:

options.label: A
options.text: Separate developers and operations into isolated silos

options.label: C
options.text: Unify software development and IT operations to deliver software faster and more reliably

explanation.why_correct: DevOps integrates development and operations (culture, practices, automation) to accelerate and stabilize software delivery.

why_others_are_wrong.A: DevOps breaks down silos rather than reinforcing them.
why_others_are_wrong.B: DevOps emphasizes automated testing, not its removal.
why_others_are_wrong.D: DevOps is about software delivery practices, not replacing software with hardware.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the dev+ops unification goal of DevOps.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Software Development Security > DevOps and DevSecOps

questions.question: Why is configuration management important to patch management during O&M?

options.label: B
options.text: It eliminates the need to ever test patches

options.label: D
options.text: It ensures patches are tracked and applied consistently against known baselines, preventing drift

explanation.why_correct: Configuration management tracks system baselines and changes, ensuring patches are applied consistently and that configuration drift/unauthorized changes are detected.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Patches still require testing.
why_others_are_wrong.C: CM exists to control changes, not permit untracked ones.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Wi-Fi encryption is unrelated to CM in patching.

questions.exam_reasoning: Connects configuration management to consistent patching.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Software Development Security > Software Operations And Maintenance

questions.question: A KEY difference between compiled and interpreted languages is that compiled languages:

options.label: A
options.text: Are always executed line-by-line from source at runtime

options.label: C
options.text: Cannot be used to build secure software

options.label: D
options.text: Are translated to machine code before execution, so the source is not distributed to run it

explanation.why_correct: Compiled languages are translated to machine code ahead of execution (the distributed artifact is the binary), while interpreted languages are translated/executed at runtime from source.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Line-by-line runtime execution describes interpreted languages.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Both compiled and interpreted languages can build secure software.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Compiled languages require compilation; interpreted require an interpreter.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes compiled (pre-translated) from interpreted (runtime) languages.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Application Security > Compiled vs. Interpreted Languages

questions.question: An interpreted application is distributed as human-readable source. From a security standpoint, what is a notable consideration?

options.label: A
options.text: It is impossible to reverse engineer in any way

options.label: C
options.text: The source code (and any embedded secrets) is readable by anyone who obtains it

options.label: D
options.text: It automatically hides all logic from users

explanation.why_correct: Interpreted code is distributed as source, so its logic—and any embedded secrets or vulnerabilities—are directly visible to anyone with the files; secrets must not be hardcoded.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Even compiled binaries can be reverse engineered; interpreted source is trivially readable.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Distributing source exposes, rather than hides, the logic.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Any code can contain vulnerabilities.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the exposure risk of distributing interpreted source.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Application Security > Compiled vs. Interpreted Languages

questions.question: In the programming language generations, which generation corresponds to machine language (binary)?

explanation.why_correct: First-generation languages (1GL) are machine language (binary) executed directly by hardware; higher generations are progressively more abstract/human-readable.

why_others_are_wrong.C: 3GLs are high-level languages (e.g., C, Java), not binary.
why_others_are_wrong.A: 4GLs are higher-level, often domain-specific languages.
why_others_are_wrong.D: 5GLs are associated with AI/constraint-based programming.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps machine language to 1GL.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Application Security > Programming Language Generations

questions.question: Reusable code libraries enhance efficiency and consistency, but from a security perspective they must be:

options.label: A
options.text: Properly managed and kept updated, since vulnerable libraries introduce supply chain risk

explanation.why_correct: Libraries speed development but can carry vulnerabilities; they must be vetted, kept updated, and tracked (supply chain risk management) to remain secure.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Outdated libraries accumulate known vulnerabilities.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Blind trust ignores supply chain risk (e.g., malicious or vulnerable components).
why_others_are_wrong.C: Libraries are valuable; the goal is secure management, not avoidance.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests secure management of code libraries.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Application Security > Code Libraries

questions.question: A Software Development Kit (SDK) typically provides:

options.label: C
options.text: Tools, libraries, and resources to build applications for a platform (sometimes including third-party resources)

options.label: D
options.text: Physical access control to the office

explanation.why_correct: An SDK bundles tools, libraries, documentation, and sometimes third-party resources to develop for a given platform; an IDE is the integrated coding environment.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Backup power is a UPS/generator function.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Physical access control is a facility control.
why_others_are_wrong.B: A wireless key is a network secret.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of the SDK's purpose.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Application Security > Software Development Kit (SDK)

questions.question: A security risk specific to SDKs that include third-party resources is that:

options.label: A
options.text: They make all code automatically secure

options.label: B
options.text: They cannot be scanned for vulnerabilities

options.label: C
options.text: They eliminate the need for testing

options.label: D
options.text: Bundled third-party components can introduce vulnerabilities or malicious code (supply chain risk)

explanation.why_correct: SDKs may include third-party libraries/components that carry their own vulnerabilities or malicious code, so they must be vetted and tracked (supply chain risk management).

why_others_are_wrong.A: Including an SDK does not guarantee security.
why_others_are_wrong.B: SDK components can and should be scanned.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Testing is still required when using SDKs.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the third-party supply chain risk of SDKs.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Application Security > Software Development Kit (SDK)

questions.question: Static Application Security Testing (SAST) analyzes:

options.label: A
options.text: A running application by sending it inputs

options.label: D
options.text: Source code or binaries WITHOUT executing the application

explanation.why_correct: SAST (white-box) examines source code/binaries without running the application, finding issues early in development.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Analyzing a running app via inputs is DAST.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Network-perimeter testing is not SAST.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Physical access logs are unrelated to SAST.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps non-executing code analysis to SAST.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Application Security > Testing Approaches

questions.question: Dynamic Application Security Testing (DAST) is BEST described as:

options.label: A
options.text: Reading source code statically without running it

options.label: D
options.text: Testing a running application from the outside (black-box) by sending inputs and observing behavior

explanation.why_correct: DAST (black-box) tests a running application by sending inputs and observing responses, finding runtime/exploitable issues.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Static source reading is SAST.
why_others_are_wrong.C: A formal inspection is a manual code review (e.g., Fagan).
why_others_are_wrong.B: A DR drill is a continuity exercise.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps running-app external testing to DAST.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Application Security > Testing Approaches

questions.question: Interactive Application Security Testing (IAST) combines aspects of SAST and DAST by:

options.label: B
options.text: Instrumenting the running application to observe code behavior during execution/testing

options.label: C
options.text: Replacing the need for all other testing

explanation.why_correct: IAST instruments the application (agents inside the running app) to observe code execution during testing, combining static insight with dynamic context.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Static-source-only analysis is SAST.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Perimeter scanning is not IAST.
why_others_are_wrong.C: IAST complements, not replaces, other testing.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the instrumented-runtime nature of IAST.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Application Security > Types of Fuzz Testing

questions.question: A tester is given full access to the application's source code and internal design to perform the assessment. This testing approach is:

explanation.why_correct: White box testing gives the tester full knowledge of internals (source, design); black box provides no internal knowledge.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Black box testing provides no internal knowledge.
why_others_are_wrong.C: A reciprocal agreement is a DR site arrangement.
why_others_are_wrong.B: A tabletop exercise is a DR test.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps full-internal-knowledge testing to white box.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Application Security > Testing Approaches

questions.question: Fuzz testing assesses software by:

options.label: D
options.text: Sending invalid, unexpected, or random inputs to find flaws or crashes

explanation.why_correct: Fuzz testing injects invalid/unexpected/random inputs to discover vulnerabilities, crashes, or unexpected behavior.

why_others_are_wrong.C: Only happy-path validation misses edge cases fuzzing targets.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Marketing plans are unrelated.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Database encryption is a separate control.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps invalid-input testing to fuzzing.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Application Security > Additional Types of Software Tests

questions.question: Mutational fuzzing generates test inputs by:

options.label: A
options.text: Building inputs from a formal model of the expected format

options.label: C
options.text: Mutating existing valid data samples into malformed variants

explanation.why_correct: Mutational fuzzing alters existing valid inputs to create malformed test cases (vs. generational/smart fuzzing, which builds inputs from a model).

why_others_are_wrong.A: Building from a model describes generational (smart) fuzzing.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Reading source only is static analysis (SAST).
why_others_are_wrong.B: Fuzzing malforms inputs; it does not encrypt them.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes mutational fuzzing (alter valid data).

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Application Security > Types of Fuzz Testing

questions.question: Match each application security testing technique (1-4) to its description (A-D).

options.label: A
options.text: Tests a running application from the outside (black-box)

options.label: B
options.text: Sends invalid/random inputs to find flaws

options.label: C
options.text: Instruments the running app to observe code during execution

explanation.why_correct: SAST → static code analysis (B); DAST → running-app black-box testing (A); IAST → instrumented runtime (D); Fuzz testing → invalid/random inputs (C).

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests mapping of application security testing techniques.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Application Security > Testing Approaches

questions.question: A critical application must defend against advanced persistent threats (APTs) with the most extensive controls. Which OWASP ASVS level applies?

explanation.why_correct: ASVS Level 3 (High) is for applications critical to operations, protecting against advanced threats including APTs, with the most extensive controls.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Level 1 (Low) is the most basic assurance level.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Level 2 (Moderate) defends against most risks but is below the APT-focused Level 3.
why_others_are_wrong.C: OWASP ASVS is a recognized standard.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps APT-grade critical apps to ASVS Level 3.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Application Security > ASVS Assurance Levels

questions.question: OWASP ASVS Level 2 (Moderate) is intended to:

options.label: A
options.text: Eliminate the need for any testing

options.label: B
options.text: Defend only against advanced persistent threats

options.label: C
options.text: Defend against most application security risks, including skilled/motivated attackers

options.label: D
options.text: Provide only the most basic assurance

explanation.why_correct: ASVS Level 2 is sufficient for most applications, defending against most risks and skilled, motivated attackers (e.g., standard pen-test resistance).

why_others_are_wrong.D: Basic assurance is Level 1.
why_others_are_wrong.B: APT-grade defense is Level 3.
why_others_are_wrong.A: ASVS guides testing requirements; it does not remove testing.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the scope of ASVS Level 2.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Application Security > ASVS Assurance Levels

questions.question: Software assurance aims to ensure that software:

options.label: A
options.text: Functions as intended while protecting against threats and vulnerabilities

options.label: B
options.text: Is the cheapest possible to produce

explanation.why_correct: Software assurance provides confidence that software functions as intended and is protected against threats/vulnerabilities.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Lowest cost is not the goal of assurance.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Marketing features are not software assurance.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Assurance relies on testing, not its absence.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the function-as-intended-and-secure goal of software assurance.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Application Security > Software Assurance

questions.question: The appropriate ASVS assurance level for an application is determined primarily by:

options.label: A
options.text: The color of the application's logo

options.label: B
options.text: The brand of the developers' laptops

options.label: C
options.text: The application's criticality and risk (informed by the SDLC)

options.label: D
options.text: The number of developers on the team

explanation.why_correct: The required assurance level is chosen based on the application's criticality and risk profile, informed by the SDLC—higher risk warrants higher assurance.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Logo color is irrelevant to assurance level.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Team size does not determine the assurance level.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Laptop brand is irrelevant.

questions.exam_reasoning: Connects ASVS level selection to criticality/risk.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Application Security > Determining Assurance Levels

questions.question: Which test verifies that two or more components work correctly TOGETHER?

explanation.why_correct: Integration testing verifies that combined components/modules interact correctly; unit testing checks a single component in isolation.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Unit testing checks one component in isolation.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Smoke testing is a quick post-build basic-functionality check.
why_others_are_wrong.C: A sanity test quickly validates a specific feature's viability.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes integration testing from unit/smoke/sanity.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Application Security > Additional Types of Software Tests

questions.question: A runtime environment provides:

options.label: A
options.text: The platform/services in which a program executes (e.g., interpreters, libraries, memory management)

options.label: C
options.text: Physical security for the data center

explanation.why_correct: A runtime environment supplies the execution platform and services (interpreters/VMs, libraries, memory management) a program relies on at run time.

why_others_are_wrong.C: Physical security is a facility control.
why_others_are_wrong.B: A generator is power equipment.
why_others_are_wrong.D: A WAP is a wireless network device.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of the runtime environment.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Application Security > Runtime Environment

questions.question: Which TWO are recognized application security testing techniques? (Select TWO.)

explanation.why_correct: SAST and DAST (along with IAST and fuzzing) are application security testing techniques.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Degaussing is a media-destruction method.
why_others_are_wrong.A: War driving is a wireless reconnaissance technique.

questions.exam_reasoning: Identifies application security testing techniques.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Application Security > Testing Approaches

questions.question: An Integrated Development Environment (IDE) primarily provides developers with:

options.label: D
options.text: A unified application combining editor, build tools, and debugger

explanation.why_correct: An IDE bundles a code editor, build/compile tools, and a debugger into one application to streamline development.

why_others_are_wrong.A: A backup power supply is a UPS/generator.
why_others_are_wrong.B: A door lock is a physical control.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Fire suppression is a physical safety control.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of the IDE.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Application Security > Software Development Kit (SDK)

questions.question: OWASP ASVS Level 1 represents:

options.label: C
options.text: The highest assurance level for APT defense

explanation.why_correct: ASVS Level 1 is the lowest, basic assurance level; Level 2 is moderate and Level 3 is high (APT-grade).

why_others_are_wrong.C: APT-grade high assurance is Level 3.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Moderate assurance is Level 2.
why_others_are_wrong.D: ASVS is an assurance standard, not a networking protocol.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of ASVS Level 1 as basic assurance.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Application Security > ASVS Assurance Levels

questions.question: A team wants to catch insecure coding patterns as early as possible during development, before the app even runs. Which testing technique fits BEST?

explanation.why_correct: SAST examines source code without execution, enabling early detection of insecure patterns during development (shift-left).

why_others_are_wrong.D: DAST requires a running application, so it is later than SAST.
why_others_are_wrong.B: A full interruption test is a DR exercise.
why_others_are_wrong.A: War driving is wireless reconnaissance, unrelated to code testing.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps earliest pre-runtime code analysis to SAST.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Application Security > Application Security Testing

questions.question: SQL injection occurs when:

options.label: B
options.text: A user changes the wireless encryption key

options.label: C
options.text: Untrusted input is included in a database query, allowing an attacker to run unauthorized SQL

explanation.why_correct: SQL injection sends crafted untrusted input that a web application incorporates into a database query, letting an attacker execute unauthorized SQL commands.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Changing a wireless key is unrelated to SQL injection.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Degaussing destroys magnetic media.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Power loss is unrelated to injection attacks.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of SQL injection.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Application Security > Injection Attacks

questions.question: A web app builds SQL queries by concatenating user input. Which control MOST directly prevents SQL injection?

options.label: C
options.text: Input validation plus parameterized queries/approved stored procedures

explanation.why_correct: Validating input and using parameterized queries/whitelisted stored procedures (so input is treated as data, not executable SQL) directly prevent SQL injection.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Disabling logging hides activity and does not prevent injection.
why_others_are_wrong.B: A faster server does not address the injection vulnerability.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Wi-Fi range is unrelated to injection defense.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps injection prevention to input validation + parameterized queries.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Application Security > Mitigations for Injection Attacks

questions.question: LDAP injection differs from SQL injection in that LDAP injection targets:

options.label: C
options.text: A directory server (e.g., LDAP/Active Directory) rather than a SQL database

explanation.why_correct: LDAP injection submits unauthorized queries to a directory server (LDAP/Active Directory); SQL injection targets relational databases; both exploit unvalidated input.

why_others_are_wrong.B: A WAP is a wireless device, not a directory server.
why_others_are_wrong.A: A generator is power equipment.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Fire suppression is a physical control.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes LDAP injection (directory) from SQL injection (database).

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Application Security > Injection Attacks

questions.question: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) primarily allows an attacker to:

options.label: C
options.text: Reformat a hard drive remotely with no access

options.label: D
options.text: Inject malicious scripts that run in other users' browsers via a vulnerable web app

explanation.why_correct: XSS injects attacker-controlled scripts that execute in victims' browsers (e.g., to steal sessions/data); output encoding and input validation mitigate it.

why_others_are_wrong.A: XSS is a web attack, not physical entry.
why_others_are_wrong.B: XSS does not drain batteries.
why_others_are_wrong.C: XSS does not reformat drives without access.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of XSS (script injection into users' browsers).

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Application Security > OWASP Top 10 Vulnerabilities

questions.question: Session hijacking takes over an active session by:

options.label: A
options.text: Stealing/replaying session tokens, cookies, or credentials

explanation.why_correct: Session hijacking uses stolen session tokens/cookies/credentials (sometimes via replay) to assume a legitimate user's active session.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Physically removing a server is theft, not session hijacking.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Degaussing destroys media.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Disabling AC is an environmental disruption, unrelated to sessions.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps stolen-token session takeover to session hijacking.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Application Security > Hijacking Attacks

questions.question: An attacker alters a file AFTER an application checks its permissions but BEFORE the application uses it, exploiting the timing gap. This is a:

explanation.why_correct: A TOCTOU attack exploits a race condition by changing a resource between the moment it is checked and the moment it is used, altering the outcome.

why_others_are_wrong.B: SQL injection manipulates database queries, not check/use timing.
why_others_are_wrong.C: XSS injects scripts into browsers.
why_others_are_wrong.A: War driving is wireless reconnaissance.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps a check-then-use race condition to TOCTOU.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Application Security > Rootkit Attacks

questions.question: Vertical privilege escalation occurs when an attacker:

options.label: B
options.text: Moves laterally to another account at the same privilege level

options.label: D
options.text: Gains higher privileges (e.g., from a normal user to administrator)

explanation.why_correct: Vertical privilege escalation raises the attacker's privilege level (e.g., user to admin); horizontal escalation moves laterally at the same level.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Same-level lateral movement is horizontal privilege escalation.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Encrypting files for ransom is ransomware.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Spam over IM is spim, unrelated to escalation.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes vertical (gain higher) from horizontal escalation.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Application Security > Rootkit Attacks

questions.question: Rootkits, which provide stealthy root/admin-level access, are BEST detected by:

explanation.why_correct: Because rootkits embed deep in the host (OS, boot sector, firmware), host-based IDS (HIDS) is best positioned to detect their presence/changes.

why_others_are_wrong.D: A fence is a physical control, irrelevant to rootkit detection.
why_others_are_wrong.C: A generator provides power.
why_others_are_wrong.B: A WAP is a wireless network device.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps rootkit detection to HIDS.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Application Security > Rootkit Attacks

questions.question: A backdoor in software is:

options.label: C
options.text: A means of bypassing normal authentication, sometimes left by developers for maintenance

explanation.why_correct: A backdoor bypasses normal authentication to grant access; developers may leave them for maintenance, but they are a serious security risk if discovered/abused.

why_others_are_wrong.D: A backdoor circumvents, rather than provides, secure authentication.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Fire suppression is a physical control.
why_others_are_wrong.B: A backdoor is not a power source.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of a backdoor (auth bypass).

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Application Security > Hijacking Attacks

questions.question: Match each application attack (1-4) to its description (A-D).

options.label: A
options.text: Runs unauthorized SQL via untrusted input

options.label: B
options.text: Exploits a race condition between check and use

options.label: C
options.text: Runs malicious scripts in other users' browsers

options.label: D
options.text: Takes over an active session using stolen tokens

explanation.why_correct: SQL injection → unauthorized SQL via input (B); XSS → scripts in users' browsers (A); TOCTOU → check/use race condition (D); Session hijacking → stolen-token session takeover (C).

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests mapping of application attacks to descriptions.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Application Security > Application Attacks

questions.question: The OWASP Top 10 is BEST described as:

options.label: D
options.text: A list of the most critical web application security risks

explanation.why_correct: The OWASP Top 10 ranks the most critical web application security risks (e.g., injection, broken access control), guiding secure development.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Wireless encryption standards are WPA2/WPA3.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Backup rotation is an operations schedule.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Physical access models are unrelated to OWASP Top 10.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of the OWASP Top 10's purpose.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Application Security > OWASP Top 10 Vulnerabilities

questions.question: A user changes the account ID in a URL and gains access to another user's data. Which OWASP category does this represent?

explanation.why_correct: Accessing another user's data by manipulating a parameter is broken access control (e.g., insecure direct object reference)—a top OWASP risk.

why_others_are_wrong.B: A backup failure is an availability/recovery issue.
why_others_are_wrong.C: A power surge is an electrical anomaly.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Wireless jamming is a network DoS.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps unauthorized data access via parameter tampering to broken access control.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Application Security > OWASP Top 10 Vulnerabilities

questions.question: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF), added in the OWASP 2021 list, allows an attacker to:

options.label: C
options.text: Make the server send crafted requests to unintended internal/external resources

explanation.why_correct: SSRF abuses a server's ability to make requests, tricking it into accessing unintended internal/external resources (e.g., internal metadata services).

why_others_are_wrong.A: SSRF is a web attack, not a physical door control.
why_others_are_wrong.B: SSRF does not encrypt backups.
why_others_are_wrong.D: SSRF does not drain batteries.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of SSRF.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Application Security > OWASP Top 10 Vulnerabilities

questions.question: Which TWO risks were notably added/elevated in the OWASP Top 10 2021 list? (Select TWO.)

explanation.why_correct: The 2021 OWASP Top 10 added insecure design and SSRF (among reorganizations); the others are physical/facility issues.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Sprinkler failure is a physical fire-safety issue.
why_others_are_wrong.A: UPS battery aging is a power-equipment concern.

questions.exam_reasoning: Identifies 2021 OWASP additions.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Application Security > OWASP Top 10 Vulnerabilities

questions.question: Which is a fundamental secure coding practice that defends against many injection attacks?

options.label: A
options.text: Hardcoding admin passwords in the source

options.label: B
options.text: Trusting all user input by default

options.label: C
options.text: Validating and sanitizing all untrusted input

explanation.why_correct: Input validation/sanitization (treating untrusted input as untrusted) is a core secure-coding practice that mitigates injection and related attacks.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Trusting all input invites injection and other attacks.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Proper error handling is itself a secure-coding practice.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Hardcoding credentials is a serious vulnerability.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps injection defense to input validation.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Application Security > Secure Coding Practices

questions.question: Proper secure error handling means an application should:

options.label: A
options.text: Fail gracefully without revealing sensitive details (e.g., stack traces) to users

options.label: D
options.text: Display full database errors and stack traces to all users

explanation.why_correct: Secure error handling avoids leaking sensitive internal details (stack traces, queries) to users while logging enough internally for diagnosis.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Exposing detailed errors aids attackers (information disclosure).
why_others_are_wrong.B: Crashing without logging removes diagnostic/audit capability.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Emailing passwords is a severe security flaw.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests secure error-handling practice.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Application Security > Secure Coding Practices

questions.question: A common API security risk highlighted in the guide is:

options.label: A
options.text: Insufficient authentication and excessive data exposure

explanation.why_correct: APIs commonly suffer from weak authentication and excessive data exposure; strong authentication, encryption, and input validation mitigate these.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Physical security is unrelated to API risk.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Generator usage is unrelated to API security.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Fire drills are a safety activity, not an API risk.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests common API security risks.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Application Security > Software API Security

questions.question: Which TWO controls help secure an API? (Select TWO.)

options.label: A
options.text: Returning all internal data by default

options.label: B
options.text: Encryption of API traffic with TLS

explanation.why_correct: APIs should enforce strong authentication and encrypt traffic (TLS), along with input validation, to limit exposure and abuse.

why_others_are_wrong.C: Open, unauthenticated access invites abuse.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Returning all internal data is excessive data exposure.

questions.exam_reasoning: Identifies sound API security controls.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Application Security > Software API Security

questions.question: Commercial Off-The-Shelf (COTS) software is:

options.label: C
options.text: Free software maintained by a community

options.label: D
options.text: Commercial software purchased and managed by the organization

explanation.why_correct: COTS is commercially available software the organization purchases and manages (e.g., a licensed productivity suite).

why_others_are_wrong.C: Community-maintained free software is OSS/FOSS.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Government-licensed software is GOTS.
why_others_are_wrong.B: A custom in-house build is bespoke development, not COTS.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of COTS.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Application Security > Types of Acquired Software

questions.question: Open-Source/Free Software (OSS/FOSS) is characterized by:

options.label: A
options.text: Always being purchased from a single commercial vendor

options.label: B
options.text: Being community-maintained and often hosted on platforms like GitHub

explanation.why_correct: OSS/FOSS is typically free, community-maintained software with available source, often hosted on platforms like GitHub.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Commercial single-vendor purchase describes COTS.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Government-only software is GOTS.
why_others_are_wrong.D: OSS makes source code available by definition.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of OSS/FOSS.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Application Security > Types of Acquired Software

questions.question: A COTS product bundles several third-party libraries (NDIs). What is the PRIMARY security concern, and the BEST response?

options.label: A
options.text: Bundled libraries are always more secure than custom code

options.label: B
options.text: There is no risk because the vendor is commercial

options.label: C
options.text: Supply chain risk from the bundled components; vet them and apply supply chain risk management

explanation.why_correct: Non-Developmental Items (NDIs)—third-party libraries bundled with products—introduce supply chain risk; they must be vetted, tracked, and managed (SCRM).

why_others_are_wrong.B: Commercial vendors' bundled components can still contain vulnerabilities.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Bundled libraries are not inherently more secure.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Third-party components require updates as vulnerabilities emerge.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps bundled third-party (NDI) risk to supply chain management.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Application Security > Types of Acquired Software

questions.question: Software acquired from the government, usually under a government license, is categorized as:

explanation.why_correct: GOTS (Government Off-The-Shelf) is software acquired from the government, typically used under a government license.

why_others_are_wrong.A: COTS is commercial purchased software.
why_others_are_wrong.B: OSS/FOSS is community-maintained free software.
why_others_are_wrong.C: NDIs are third-party components bundled into other products.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of GOTS.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Application Security > Types of Acquired Software

questions.question: A security-focused software acquisition policy should ensure the organization:

options.label: B
options.text: Buys whichever software is cheapest with no security review

options.label: C
options.text: Communicates security/compliance requirements to vendors and applies supply chain risk management

options.label: D
options.text: Never tests acquired software before deployment

explanation.why_correct: A sound acquisition policy communicates security/compliance requirements (e.g., GDPR, HIPAA) to vendors, uses trusted vendors, and applies SCRM—especially for bundled NDIs.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Cheapest-with-no-review ignores security risk.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Acquired software should be tested before production.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Vendors should be evaluated, not blindly trusted.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the elements of a secure acquisition policy.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Application Security > Security Considerations for Acquired Software

questions.question: Per NIST acquisition guidance, an organization confirms a provider meets its security needs BEFORE finalizing the purchase. Which step is this?

explanation.why_correct: In the NIST acquisition approach (Preparation, Selection, Agreement Management, Monitoring, Acceptance), Acceptance confirms compliance with security needs before purchasing/licensing.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Preparation defines security needs and includes them in requests.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Selection evaluates vendors for trustworthiness.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Monitoring assesses ongoing performance/SLA adherence after acquisition.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps pre-purchase compliance confirmation to the Acceptance step.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Application Security > NIST Acquisition Controls

questions.question: In the SaaS model for acquired software, the customer is primarily responsible for:

options.label: A
options.text: Its own data and access controls (the provider manages the OS and supporting applications)

options.label: B
options.text: Maintaining the provider's physical data center

options.label: C
options.text: Writing the SaaS application's source code

explanation.why_correct: In SaaS, the provider manages the OS and supporting applications, while the customer manages its data and access controls.

why_others_are_wrong.D: OS patching is the provider's responsibility in SaaS.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Physical data-center maintenance is the provider's responsibility.
why_others_are_wrong.C: The provider develops/maintains the SaaS application.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests SaaS customer responsibilities (data + access).

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Application Security > Cloud-Based Lease Software Models

questions.question: Before deploying acquired software to production, a best practice is to:

options.label: A
options.text: Assume it is secure because it was purchased

options.label: B
options.text: Deploy it immediately with no evaluation

options.label: D
options.text: Conduct security testing (e.g., vulnerability and privacy impact assessments)

explanation.why_correct: Acquired software should undergo security testing (vulnerability assessments, privacy impact assessments) before production and be monitored continuously afterward.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Immediate deployment without evaluation risks importing vulnerabilities.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Purchased software is not automatically secure.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Monitoring is needed to catch emerging issues.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests pre-deployment security testing of acquired software.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Application Security > Best Practices for Acquired Software

questions.question: Which TWO are categories of acquired software described in the guide? (Select TWO.)

explanation.why_correct: COTS and OSS/FOSS are acquired-software categories (along with GOTS and NDIs); TOCTOU and XSS are attack types.

why_others_are_wrong.D: TOCTOU is a race-condition attack.
why_others_are_wrong.C: XSS is a web application attack.

questions.exam_reasoning: Separates acquired-software categories from attack types.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Application Security > Types of Acquired Software

questions.question: Which TWO are risks included in the OWASP Top 10? (Select TWO.)

explanation.why_correct: Injection and broken access control are OWASP Top 10 web application security risks; the others are physical/facility issues.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Backup tape aging is a media/operations concern, not an OWASP risk.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Air-conditioning failure is an environmental issue, not an OWASP risk.

questions.exam_reasoning: Identifies OWASP Top 10 risks.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Application Security > OWASP Top 10 Vulnerabilities

questions.question: Domain hijacking involves:

options.label: C
options.text: Unauthorized changes to a domain's registration/DNS records to redirect traffic

explanation.why_correct: Domain hijacking makes unauthorized changes to registered domain records (e.g., DNS) to redirect traffic to attacker-controlled destinations.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Stealing a session cookie is session hijacking.
why_others_are_wrong.D: SQL injection targets databases, not domain records.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Draining a UPS is unrelated to domain hijacking.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes domain hijacking from session hijacking.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Application Security > Hijacking Attacks

questions.question: To mitigate the OWASP Top 10 across an application, the MOST effective approach is to:

options.label: A
options.text: Add a single firewall rule and consider the app secure

options.label: C
options.text: Apply secure coding practices (input validation, output encoding, parameterization, error handling) throughout development

options.label: D
options.text: Rely solely on a post-release penetration test

explanation.why_correct: Building secure coding practices into development (validation, encoding, parameterized queries, proper error handling) addresses the root causes behind the OWASP Top 10.

why_others_are_wrong.A: A single firewall rule does not address application-layer code flaws.
why_others_are_wrong.D: A post-release pen test alone is too late and not comprehensive.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Hardcoding credentials introduces a serious vulnerability.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps broad OWASP mitigation to integrated secure coding.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Application Security > Secure Coding Practices

questions.question: Broken authentication (an OWASP Top 10 risk) typically results from:

options.label: A
options.text: Poorly managed credentials, sessions, or authentication logic

explanation.why_correct: Broken authentication stems from weaknesses in credential, session, or authentication management (e.g., weak passwords, exposed session IDs), enabling account compromise.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Backup power is unrelated to authentication.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Fire drills are a safety activity.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Strict input validation strengthens, not breaks, security.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the causes of broken authentication.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Application Security > OWASP Top 10 Vulnerabilities

questions.question: In a PaaS model, the customer typically:

options.label: A
options.text: Has no responsibility for the application

options.label: D
options.text: Owns the application (with some limited control over its security) while the provider manages the OS

explanation.why_correct: In PaaS, the provider manages the OS/platform while the customer owns the application (with limited control over underlying security).

why_others_are_wrong.B: Physical facilities are the provider's responsibility.
why_others_are_wrong.A: The customer owns/operates the application in PaaS.
why_others_are_wrong.C: OS patching is the provider's responsibility in PaaS.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests PaaS customer responsibilities (the application).

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 8 > Application Security > Cloud-Based Lease Software Models
